newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Hanoi kick-starts drive for education, technology.
newsitem.headline: Hanoi kick-starts drive for education, technology.

text.p: The Central Committee of Vietnam's Communist Party has agreed on a drive to improve the country's technological know-how and cash-strapped education system, official media reports said on Thursday.
The 170-strong committee, gathering for a year-end meeting behind closed doors, also focused on training and science and touched on the problems of corruption and bureaucracy.

However, reports of the eight-day "plenum" were short on detail and there was no mention of a replacement for Nguyen Dinh Tu, who has been selected to join the inner Politburo in June but died before he could take his seat.
Another Politburo member, President Le Duc Anh, has been incapacitated by a stroke, and political sources say he is not expected to recover sufficiently to resume his duties.

Analysts said that although the plenum would not normally be a forum for formal discussion of leadership issues, it was likely that the question of who should replace the 76-year-old army general -- and when -- was broached.

Party Secretary General Do Muoi, one of a leadership troika with Anh and Prime Minister Vo Van Kiet, said in an opening speech to the plenum that 10 years of economic reform had still left the country deficient in education, training and technology.

"It is necessary to consider education as the most important basic investment for overall development of the country," he said, calling for universalisation of primary education and an end to illiteracy by the turn of the century.
Vietnam's 75 million people are better educated than those of most other low-income nations. According to a United Nations report, the adult literacy rate in 1993 was 92.5 percent.

However, the government has stopped covering all the costs of education since the implementation of economic reforms 10 years ago, which has made it particularly hard for the poor to send their children to school.
"Financial pressures on local budgets have obliged schools to charge de facto user fees for even primary education," the U.N. said in a recent report.
It said poor families now faced costs no longer paid for by the state such as transport and books, as well as the fear of losing potential earnings from putting their children to work.
There are 1.8 million children of primary school age not in school in Vietnam and, according to the United Nations, 24 percent of all nine-year-olds are employed in some capacity other than at home.

Another concern is the quality and quantity of teachers. Official media reports have put the teacher shortage at 100,000, and the government is looking at ways of attracting educated people to a profession that pays less than $30 a month.
A well-known academic from Can Tho university, Vo Tong Xuan, said in a highly critical interview with the Saigon Economic Times this week that the quality of education had slipped too far.
"I suggest that the Party have a second revolution. The first revolution was economic; it has been done," he said. "The second revolution should be for education and training."
